power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

report: Reporting *p* values imprecisely (e.g., *p* < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in *p* value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").

text.text: Background and Objectives: Multiple sclerosis (MS) is a chronic neurological disorder characterized by demyelination and neuroaxonal injury.
Genetics of MS susceptibility and long term disability is well characterized, but the genetic contribution to disability recorded earlier in the disease course is uncertain.

We performed common-variant associations with the early period MS severity to identify potential causal loci, effector genes and associated pathways, and understand the relationships of early MS severity and other traits.

Methods: The primary outcome was the first age-related MS severity score (ARMSS), an ageadjusted severity measure, in 7,209 individuals of Swedish discovery cohorts and independent Italian and multi-national European replication cohorts.
Replicated loci underwent conditional analysis, finemapping, time-to-event MS phenotype association analyses, and multi-omics-integrated gene prioritization.

Using the genome-wide summary statistics, we also conducted heritability analyses, polygenic risk score association with MS susceptibility and late MS severity, gene-level analyses, cross-trait analyses, Mendelian randomization, and drug-repurposing screening.

Results: Two suggestive loci were replicated: rs1234317 on chromosome 1 (effect allele T: beta = 0.100, SE = 0.0189, P = 1.08 × 10 -7 ) and rs929769 on chromosome 5 (effect allele T: beta = -0.0956, SE = 0.0184, P = 1.95 × 10 -7 ).
Fine-mapping supported rs929769 strongly in chromosome 5, and rs1234317 and rs6657136 in chromosome 1 with lower confidence.
The SNPs did not show a significant change in effect sizes when adjusted for heritable traits and exhibited attenuated associations with long-term MS disability progression.
TNFSF4 was the top prioritized effector for rs1234317, TNFSF18 for rs6657136, and ADAMTS2 for rs929769.

Early MS severity showed partial genetic overlap with MS susceptibility and late MS severity, but no significant correlation with a range of neurological, psychiatric, autoimmune, cognitive, and aging traits.
Pathway analyses identified ion-channel regulation and folic acid metabolism.
Mendelian randomization suggested nominal bidirectional causal associations with educational attainment.
In silico drug screening nominated several candidate drugs.
Discussion: This study identifies candidate causal variants of early MS severity and their effector genes: TNFSF4, TNFSF18, and ADAMTS2.
It provides insights into the genetic architecture and therapeutic measures for the early phase of MS severity.
NOTE: This preprint reports new research that has not been certified by peer review and should not be used to guide clinical practice.
Multiple sclerosis (MS) involves immune infiltration of the central nervous system (CNS), leading to neurological disability.
Interplay between genetic and lifestyle factors shapes susceptibility to MS.

The Human Leukocyte Antigen (HLA) region has the strongest genetic effect 1 on disease susceptibility, whereas >200 additional non-HLA loci contribute modest to small effects. 2 Although many genetic risk factors for MS susceptibility have been identified, disease severity remains largely underexplored.

text.text: Since the existing genome-wide association study (GWAS) on MS severity focused on the late disease phase, we aimed to elucidate the genetic architecture of the disease severity of the early phase of MS.

In addition to GWAS, we conducted fine-mapping for causal variants identification, association analyses with time-to-event MS phenotypes of the replicated SNPs (eFigure 1), integration of multi-omics gene prioritization, and tissue-specific gene expression and gene-set enrichment analyses.
We further examined genetic correlations with various traits, assessed causal traits in relation to early MS severity, and potential therapeutic compounds.

Given that treatment development supported by genetics significantly increases the potential of success, 7 our findings offer mechanistic insights and help in patient care in the early period of MS disability progression.

Replication analysis was performed in the same regression model and the single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) were considered successfully replicated if the significance level of the one-sided P-value was below 0.05 with concordant direction of effect.

text.text: To estimate SNP-based heritability, we used pooled genotype data of the discovery and replication populations and calculated a genomic relationship matrix (GRM) after cohortlevel quality control and harmonization to a common autosomal biallelic SNP set.
Variants were trimmed with minor allele frequency (MAF) >= 0.01, genotype missingness <= 0.02 from the autosome.

We fine-mapped the two replicated loci using 1Mb windows around the lead variants.
Summary statistics from the meta-analysis platforms were intersected with genotype data from all the cohorts.
Platform-specific LD matrices were calculated after residualizing the genotypes for study-specific covariates and combined using sample-size weighting.
Kriging diagnostics and λs_rss were calculated to support the use of the weighted sum LD matrix.
We utilized two methods for robustness: SuSiE-RSS 18 and FINEMAP v1.4 19 allowing up to 10 causal variants.

The time-to-event disability analyses examined three traits: rate of Expanded Disability Status Scale (EDSS) progression over disease duration using a generalized linear mixed model (GLMM), time to clinically meaningful worsening (24-week confirmed disability worsening, Cox proportional hazards), and time to EDSS 6.0 with sensitivity analysis as time to sustained EDSS 6.0, both using interval-censored Cox model.

Candidate effector genes were prioritized using an integrative SNP-to-gene framework applied to the SNPs of interest and their LD proxies from the 1000 Genomes phase 3 European reference panel (r2 ≥ 0.6).

text.text: We then tested each SNP in linear mixed models and did not find notable difference in effect size or statistical significance compared to main analysis.
We also conducted linear regression without RINT for clinical interpretability, which exhibited significance in effects (eTable 7).
In addition, for these three SNPs we adjusted for several traits: age at onset, disease duration at first EDSS, and ever-smoking history to detect any confounding effects.
No evidence of collider biases was observed and all three SNPs remained significant and similar in effect sizes after adjustments (eTable 8, eFigure 6).

We next examined whether the prioritized SNPs affect MS progression using three disability accumulation MS phenotypes: rate of EDSS progression, time to 24-week confirmed worsening, and time to EDSS 6 with interval censoring.
Time to sustained EDSS 6 was a sensitivity analysis of time to EDSS 6.
Overall, associations with MS disability accumulations were weaker and less consistent.

The rs1234317_T allele was associated with shorter time to EDSS ≥ 6 (HR = 1.15, SE = 0.0504, P = 0.00688), and rs929769_C was associated with higher EDSS scores over disease duration (β = 0.159, SE = 0.0472, P = 0.0007).
No variant showed consistent evidence of altered EDSS progression rate or 24week confirmed disability worsening.
Full per-variant analyses of the tested MS progression phenotypes are provided in eFigures 7-9 and eSuppplementary.
Integrative SNP-to-gene prioritization of 23 LD proxies for the three candidate causal variants are shown in eTable 9 and were used for prioritizing the potential effector genes.
TNFSF4 was prioritized for rs1234317 based on positional, cS2G, and L2G evidence.
The bulk and single-cell RNA-seq annotations for TNFSF4 supported its expression in immune and CNS-relevant cell types.
TNFSF18 was prioritized for rs6657136 in positional, eQTL, and chromatin-interaction mapping.
The TNFSF18 expression was found across brain tissues and neuronal, macrophage/microglial, and glial populations.
ADAMTS2 was prioritized for rs929769 based on positional and cS2G evidence.
Its expression was seen in fibroblasts, macrophages, oligodendroglial cells, and neuronal clusters.
Detailed geneprioritization scores, expression profiles, eQTL results, and chromatin-interaction annotations are in eSupplementary text, eTable 9, and eFigures 10-12.
Genome-wide gene-association scan and pathway analyses provided suggestive support for biological pathways relevant to early MS severity.
Although MAGMA did not identify FDR-significant genes, LDAK-KVIK-GBAT identified 189 FDR-significant genes associated with early MS severity (eFigure 13, eTables 10-11).

Tissue-specific expression analyses demonstrated enrichment of the FDR-significant genes among downregulated differentially expressed genes (DEGs) in brain regions, upregulated DEGs in EBVtransformed lymphocytes, and bidirectional DEGs in the left ventricle (eFigures 14-15, eTables 12-13).
Pathway analyses highlighted sinoatrial node cell development and differentiation, cardiac pacemaker cell differentiation, folic acid transport, and folic acid binding (eTables 14-18, eFigure 16).
The full results are in eSupplementary.
Genetic overlap analyses suggested partial but limited sharing between early MS severity, MS susceptibility, and late MS severity.

Phenome-wide lookup of rs929769, rs6657136, and rs1234317 found no significant evidence of pleiotropic associations and genome-wide cross-trait analyses reported limited shared genetic contributions of early MS severity with broader neurological, psychiatric, cognitive, autoimmune, or aging-related traits (eTable 26; eFigure 18).

In two-sample MR analyses, we found no evidence of causal or reverse-causal associations for 25-hydroxyvitamin D, body mass index, or lifetime smoking index, although the reverse analysis for lifetime smoking showed heterogeneity (P = 5.3 × 10 -4 ).

Higher educational attainment suggested a nominal inverse causal association with early MS severity across the MR estimators, with no evidence of directional pleiotropy by Egger intercept (P = 0.732 and 0.346) or MR-PRESSO global tests (P = 0.201 and 0.091).
Reverse MR for educational attainment also suggested a nominal causal association (β = -0.0755, SE = 0.0327, P = 0.0209), with acceptable heterogeneity (P = 0.253; Figure 3; eTables 27-28).

We conducted a GWAS of early MS severity using the first ARMSS measurement to characterize disability at an early stage when long-term progression and cumulative treatment exposure have not dominated the phenotype.

Disability accumulation in MS involves two partially separable processes: relapse-associated worsening (RAW) that predominates early, and progression independent of relapse activity (PIRA) that contributes increasingly as the disease evolves. 24 Our study design leveraged early ARMSS and excluded measurements proximal to relapses, to reduce the relapse-driven disability dominance but retain sensitivity to early PIRA-related disability accrual.

text.text: We identified two replicated loci, at chromosomes 1 and 5, and fine-mapping prioritized rs1234317, rs6657136, and rs929769 as candidate causal variants.
Integrative gene prioritization nominated TNFSF4, TNFSF18, and ADAMTS2 .
We also observed partial overlap of early MS severity genetics with MS susceptibility and less with late severity, but limited overlap with broader disease-related traits.
Potential bidirectional causal relationship was indicated between early MS severity and the education years, and several pathways and drug candidates were suggested.

Although SNP-heritability estimates was barely crossing the borderline null value in 95% CI, the results imply common-variant contribution to early MS severity, which could be detected with larger participant size.

Fine-mapping provided the strongest support for rs929769 at chromosome 5, whereas chromosome 1 locus demonstrated rs6657136 and rs1234317 as the most probable causal SNPs yet with lower confidence shown by large number of variants in the second credible set.
Sensitivity analyses confirmed the effect of all three SNPs.
The attenuated associations of these variants with later time-to-event disability outcomes suggest that their effects may be more relevant to early severity than to long-term disability accumulation.
Integrative multi-omics-based candidate effector gene investigation prioritized TNFSF4, TNFSF18, and ADAMTS2.
TNFSF4 encodes OX40L, a regulator of T-cell activation.

Astrocytic OX40L can stimulate OX40-positive T cells in CNS tissue, promoting glial activation, blood-brain barrier (BBB) breakdown, and axonal damage. [25] [26] [27] TNFSF18 encodes glucocorticoid-induced TNFR-related protein (GITR) ligand (GITRL) expressed in immune and CNS-resident cell types and participates in regulatory T-cell expansion, CNS neuroinflammatory signaling. 28, 29 ADAMTS2 encodes a secreted metalloprotease involved in extracellular matrix (ECM) remodeling, with expression localized to excitatory neurons and perivascular fibroblast-like cells.

text.text: Genetic comparison with MS susceptibility and late MS severity suggested partial but limited overlap.

Although the selected susceptibility and late-severity variants were associated with early MS severity and non-random concordance in effect direction between early severity and MS susceptibility was detected, early severity did not show the immunecell or CNS-cell heritability enrichment patterns observed for MS susceptibility and late severity, respectively.

This could be due to early severity not being driven by either mechanism or power issue. 2, 3 However, early severity regressed on PGS constructed by the two phenotypes explained little additional variance.

text.text: Collectively, these findings suggest that early MS severity may share selected genetic components with MS susceptibility and later disability severity, but to limited extent.

In examining the genetic relationships of early MS severity with various phenotypes, neither phenome-wide analyses for rs929769, rs6657136, and rs1234317, nor genomewide genetic correlations with neurological, psychiatric, aging, and autoimmune traits revealed significant associations.

The results could be due to early severity having unique genetic architecture or limitation in heritability estimates due to available sample size. 33 Secondary overrepresentation analyses of early MS severity GWGAS genes in tissues and cell-specific DEGs may reflect shared transcriptional characteristics with reduced expression in brain tissues, active expression in immune cells, and cellular energy metabolism or stress response signatures across excitable cell types.

text.text: Educational attainment suggested a nominal bidirectional causal association with early MS severity.

This bidirectional outputs align with the broader concept of cognitive reserve and resilience, in which higher educational attainment may buffer against cognitive damage. 41, 42 Conversely, genetic variants that accelerate early disease severity may influence neural integrity in prodromal and early phase of MS during adolescence and early adulthood, leading to cognitive difficulties and having fewer years of education. 43 In silico drug-prioritization analyses nominated compounds targeting the GWASprioritized genes TNFSF4, TNFSF18, and ADAMTS2.

text.text: Despite the drug-gene link are more of hypothesis-generating, the findings narrow down the candidate drug and therapeutic components that could be informative in further validation experiments to establishing disease modifying treatment in MS.
This study has limitations.
First, all participants were of European genetic ancestry, limiting generalizability to other ancestries.
Second, relapse status at the time of EDSS assessment was unavailable in the Italian cohort during the data analyses phase.
However, EDSS measurements were clinically guided to be conducted outside periods of recent relapse.

Approximately 1.7% of the EDSS measurements (discovery: 116/5593, replication: 4/1616) may have been used in the late MS severity GWAS, since the individuals (N = 120) had only one measurement recorded in the registries.
However, the minimal overlap suggests a negligible impact on our findings.
Finally, in MR analyses, instrumental variable assumption violation cannot be fully excluded, despite our sensitivity MR analyses displayed no sign of horizontal pleiotropy.
In conclusion, our study provides insight into the genetic architecture of early MS severity and nominates effector biology for functional follow-ups.
Further experimental work is needed to clarify the mechanism and evaluate therapeutic relevance for the early stages of MS.
